extracted.intended_audience: readers and contributors of The Spectator; writers and critics of polite literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and moral/style principles for writing Spectator-style essays and for conduct in courtship, marriage, family life, and modest living as articulated in Addison & Steele's Spectator papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid news, politics, and party
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should contain 'not in it a single Word of News, a Reflection in Politics, nor a Stroak of Party.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from reporting news or taking partisan political positions; prefer subjects that do not inflame party divisions. The editor argues this keeps the paper temperate and broadly acceptable while still popular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject loose, immoral, or obscene matter and private scandal
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'fashionable Touches of Infidelity, no obscene Ideas, no Satyrs upon Priesthood, Marriage, and the like popular Topics of Ridicule; no private Scandal, nor any Thing that may tend to the Defamation of particular Persons, Families, or Societies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use salacious, irreligious, or scandalous content merely to sell copy; such methods are 'mean and base' and are intentionally rejected in favour of content that improves mind and morals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect private reputation; avoid implying real persons
rubrics_metrics.description: When drawing a faulty character, consider all those persons the malice of the world may apply it to; choose imaginary names carefully so they 'may not bear any Resemblance' to real people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine all particulars (circumstances, names, letters) to ensure no reasonable person can take the piece as aimed at a real individual; dash characters with particular circumstances to prevent ill-natured applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid offending high public figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Take care 'not to give Offence to those who appear in the higher Figures of Life' and refrain from making merry at the expense of public characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even potentially ludicrous material (e.g., public processions) may be left untouched to avoid unnecessary offence; the paper should not trade reputation or civility for cheap humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a temperate, non-partisan tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should 'draw Mens Minds off from the Bitterness of Party, and furnish them with Subjects of Discourse that may be treated without Warmth or Passion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select topics and a tone that allow civil, reflective discussion rather than heated debate; emulate examples (like the Royal Society) that redirected contentious minds toward innocuous, improving amusements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism should discover beauties, not merely expose faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques are written 'with an Intention rather to discover Beauties and Excellencies in the Writers of my own Time, than to publish any of their Faults and Imperfections.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When performing literary criticism, aim to highlight overlooked merits as well as defects. Be impartial: critique the author’s work without attacking the person, and be willing to have other critics present alternative readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present judgments as private opinion and invite candour
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish criticism 'only deliver it as my private Opinion' and accept that 'Criticism is of a very large Extent, and every particular Master in this Art has his favourite Passages.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame evaluations humbly (as personal view), encourage others to share better remarks ('Si quid novisti rectius istis, Candidus imperti'), and avoid imposing a single canon of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful drafting to avoid legal or moral offence
rubrics_metrics.description: Take pains 'in qualifying what I write... that nothing may be interpreted as aimed at private Persons' and run over in one's mind eminent persons who might be implicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before publishing, mentally test whether characters, descriptions, or names could be read as targeting real individuals or groups; alter particulars accordingly to avert defamation or undue offence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value long courtship and the growth of affection
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Those Marriages generally abound most with Love and Constancy, that are preceded by a long Courtship. The Passion should strike Root, and gather Strength before Marriage be grafted on it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage extended courtship so affection can mature and fix the idea of the beloved in the mind; long hopes and expectations habituate fondness and better support durable marriage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose spouse for character over mere beauty or fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'a Woman that is agreeable in my own Eye, and not deformed in that of the World' and value 'Good-Nature and Evenness of Temper... Virtue and good Sense... Love and Constancy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise kindness, temper, virtue, and good sense above dazzling beauty or mere estate; practical qualities sustain affection and domestic harmony better than showy appearances or wealth alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be inquisitive about faults before marriage; be lenient afterward
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Before Marriage we cannot be too inquisitive and discerning in the Faults of the Person beloved, nor after it too dim-sighted and superficial.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate and understand a partner’s faults prior to committing; once married, employ discretion and benevolence so imperfections are softened into agreeable traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise different kinds of marriages and seek the happy mix
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Marriage of Love is pleasant; a Marriage of Interest easie; and a Marriage, where both meet, happy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand whether a proposed match is motivated by affection, advantage, or both; strive for a union that combines mutual affection with reasonable provision for shared life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate reciprocal respect and duties between parents and children
rubrics_metrics.description: Fathers and sons should remember their earlier positions and obligations: 'If every Father remembered his own Thoughts and Inclinations when he was a Son, and every Son remembered what he expected from his Father... this one Reflection would preserve Men.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage mutual forbearance: parents exercise reason and temper in authority, and children temper youthful impulses with deference, preserving family harmony across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: True retirement requires renouncing desire for notoriety
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The best way of separating a Man's self from the World, is to give up the Desire of being known to it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one wishes a quiet, self-directed life, the crucial change is inner — abandoning the wish to be publicly known or applauded; perform duties and enjoy private pleasures without seeking public display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish genuine modesty/charity from mere affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise is due to the Humourist who gives away surplus to help the afflicted; conversely, beware of people who assume singular habits out of mere contradiction (e.g., those who affect closeness or poverty to be peculiar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admire authentic modesty and generosity enacted by those who quietly relieve need; distrust behaviours rooted in ostentation, obstinacy, or calculated mannerisms (the example of 'Irus' illustrates feigned closeness/covetousness as manipulative).
